fragments.text: First calculate averages for successive four-period blocks. Because four is an even number, each average falls between actual time periods; centre it by averaging adjacent four-period moving averages. This produces a trend value aligned with an actual period.

fragments.label: Qualitative forecasting
fragments.text: Uses expert judgement, sales-force/customer insight, Delphi-style opinion or market knowledge when reliable historical data are limited or conditions are changing. It captures factors a time series may miss but is subjective.

Marketing strategy coordinates objectives, research, resources and the marketing mix into a coherent plan. You must understand marketing plans, make consistent strategic choices, analyse IT/AI, and evaluate international market selection, entry methods and standardisation versus local adaptation.

fragments.label: Marketing plan
fragments.text: A documented set of marketing objectives, research, budgets/resources, actions and controls.

fragments.label: Positioning
fragments.text: The intended perception of a product/brand relative to alternatives in the target customer's mind.

fragments.label: Market entry strategy
fragments.text: Method used to enter a foreign market, e.g. exporting, licensing/franchising, joint venture or direct investment.

fragments.label: Pan-global strategy
fragments.text: A largely standardised marketing approach across countries.

fragments.label: Local adaptation
fragments.text: Changing the offer/marketing mix for local culture, law or market conditions.

fragments.label: Marketing planning
fragments.text: A plan converts objectives into target markets, budgets, responsibilities, mix decisions and controls. It improves coordination and measurement but can become rigid or outdated if assumptions/data change quickly.

fragments.label: Coordinated strategy
fragments.text: Segmentation, targeting and positioning should guide product, price, promotion and distribution. The mix must be internally consistent and feasible within finance/operations resources. A premium position combined with constant deep discounting can damage coherence.

fragments.label: IT and AI
fragments.text: Digital platforms support CRM, recommendations, automated advertising, personalisation, dynamic analysis and experimentation. Benefits include targeting and measurable data; risks include privacy, algorithmic bias, inaccurate data, cybersecurity and platform dependence.

fragments.label: Selecting international markets
fragments.text: Assess size/growth, income, culture, competition, regulation, political/economic risk, distribution, exchange rates and strategic fit. A large market is not automatically attractive if entry barriers/adaptation costs are high.

fragments.label: Entry modes
fragments.text: Exporting requires lower commitment/control; licensing/franchising can expand quickly but sacrifices control/know-how; joint ventures provide local knowledge while sharing control/profit; wholly owned investment gives high control but requires high capital and risk exposure.

fragments.label: Standardisation versus adaptation
fragments.text: Pan-global standardisation can reduce design/promotion cost and create consistent brand identity. Local adaptation improves cultural/legal relevance but raises complexity/cost. The best balance depends on similarity of customer needs and regulation.
entry mode trades control vs capital/risk

Location and scale shape cost, responsiveness, risk and long-run competitiveness. You must analyse local/national/international location decisions, offshoring and reshoring, globalisation, and internal/external economies and diseconomies of scale.

fragments.label: Offshoring
fragments.text: Moving business activities or production to another country.

fragments.label: Reshoring
fragments.text: Returning previously offshored activity to the home country.

fragments.label: Economies of scale
fragments.text: Reductions in average/unit cost as scale increases.

fragments.label: Diseconomies of scale
fragments.text: Increases in average/unit cost caused by excessive size/complexity.

fragments.label: External economies
fragments.text: Cost advantages gained because the industry/region grows, not because one firm alone becomes larger.

fragments.label: Location factors
fragments.text: Important factors include labour skill/cost, land/rent, suppliers, transport, infrastructure, energy, customers, government incentives/tax, law/political stability and sustainability. Weighting depends on the business model—a data centre, luxury retailer and heavy manufacturer should not prioritise the same factors.

fragments.label: Offshoring
fragments.text: Can lower labour/input cost, access specialist suppliers and place production nearer growing markets. Risks include longer supply chains, quality/control problems, exchange/political risk, cultural/communication issues and reputational concerns.

fragments.label: Reshoring
fragments.text: May improve responsiveness, quality control, supply-chain resilience and home-market reputation. It can also increase direct labour/property cost. Automation can make reshoring more viable by reducing labour-cost differences.

fragments.label: Globalisation and location
fragments.text: Trade liberalisation, digital coordination and global logistics allow firms to split design, production and service across countries. This increases choice but also creates dependence on international networks exposed to tariffs, pandemics, geopolitical tension and currency movement.

fragments.label: Internal economies of scale
fragments.text: Purchasing (bulk discounts), technical (specialised machinery), managerial (specialist managers), financial (access/cost of finance), marketing (spread fixed promotion cost) and risk-bearing/diversification can reduce unit cost as the firm grows.

fragments.label: External economies and diseconomies
fragments.text: Industry clusters can provide specialist labour, suppliers, infrastructure and knowledge. But very large businesses may suffer communication, coordination, motivation and bureaucracy problems, causing unit costs to rise. Growth is beneficial only while economies outweigh diseconomies.

Quality management aims to deliver outputs fit for purpose and consistent with customer expectations. You must distinguish quality control, quality assurance and Total Quality Management and explain how benchmarking can identify performance gaps and support improvement.

fragments.label: Quality control
fragments.text: Inspection/testing of output to identify defects, often after or at stages of production.

fragments.label: Quality assurance
fragments.text: Systems and procedures designed to prevent defects by building quality into processes.

fragments.label: TQM
fragments.text: A whole-organisation culture of continuous quality improvement where everyone is responsible for quality.

fragments.label: Benchmarking
fragments.text: Comparing performance/processes with a strong external or internal reference to identify improvement gaps.

fragments.label: Continuous improvement
fragments.text: Ongoing repeated efforts to improve process, quality, cost or customer value.

fragments.label: Why quality matters
fragments.text: Consistent quality can reduce returns/rework, strengthen reputation, support repeat purchase and premium positioning, and reduce waste. But 'maximum specification' is not always optimal if customers will not pay for it; quality is about meeting target expectations reliably.

fragments.label: Quality control
fragments.text: Inspection detects defects before they reach customers and provides measurable standards. It can be expensive and often finds errors after resources have already been wasted; responsibility may become concentrated in inspectors rather than the workforce.

fragments.label: Quality assurance
fragments.text: Standards, procedures, training and process checks aim to prevent errors at source. It can improve consistency and reduce rework but requires design, documentation, staff commitment and supplier consistency.

fragments.label: Total Quality Management
fragments.text: TQM makes quality everyone's responsibility and emphasises customer focus, prevention and continuous improvement. Potential gains include lower defect cost and stronger culture; barriers include training/time cost, employee resistance and difficulty maintaining commitment.

fragments.label: Benchmarking process
fragments.text: Identify what to improve, select a comparator/best practice, measure gaps, understand the reasons, adapt practices, implement and review. It can provide external targets but data may be unavailable and blindly copying another firm can fail because objectives/resources differ.

fragments.label: Quality and finance/strategy
fragments.text: Quality investment can raise short-run costs but reduce warranty, scrap and complaint costs and improve demand/reputation. The judgement depends on defect cost, customer expectations, competitive position and required investment.

Operations strategy turns resources and processes into long-term capability. The current syllabus includes resource constraints, flexibility, process innovation, IT/AI, ERP, lean production and Critical Path Analysis (CPA). This topic is highly integrative because operations choices depend on HR, marketing and finance.

fragments.label: ERP
fragments.text: Enterprise Resource Planning: an integrated information system linking major business functions through shared data.

fragments.label: Lean production
fragments.text: An approach that seeks customer value using less waste, delay, inventory and non-value activity.

fragments.label: JIT
fragments.text: Just-in-time: materials/components arrive close to when needed, minimising inventory.

fragments.label: Critical path
fragments.text: The sequence of zero-total-float activities determining minimum project duration.

fragments.label: Total float
fragments.text: How long an activity can be delayed without delaying overall project completion.

fragments.label: Free float
fragments.text: How long an activity can be delayed without delaying the earliest start of a following activity.

fragments.label: Resource constraints and flexibility
fragments.text: Operations decisions depend on available finance, skilled labour and expected demand. Flexibility may mean changing volume, delivery time or specification quickly. It can improve customer response but may require spare capacity, multi-skilled employees, adaptable equipment or responsive suppliers—all with costs.

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: Automation, sensors, predictive maintenance, scheduling systems and AI can improve speed, consistency and information. Risks include capital cost, cybersecurity, skill shortages, inaccurate models and reduced flexibility if technology is too specialised.

fragments.label: ERP
fragments.text: ERP links purchasing, inventory, sales, finance, HR and production to shared real-time data. It can reduce duplicated entry and improve planning/coordination. Implementation can be expensive and disruptive; poor data, weak training or badly redesigned processes can cause failure.

fragments.label: Lean production tools
fragments.text: Kaizen = continuous small improvements; quality circles = employee groups solving process/quality issues; simultaneous engineering = functions/stages work in parallel; cell production = teams handle a family of products; JIT reduces inventory; waste management removes non-value activity.

fragments.label: Lean trade-offs
fragments.text: Low inventory cuts holding cost and exposes problems but increases dependence on reliable suppliers/transport. Employee involvement can improve ideas/motivation but change may create resistance. Lean should reduce waste, not blindly remove every buffer needed for resilience.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis
fragments.text: Create the network, calculate earliest/latest times, identify activities with zero total float and find minimum duration. Float helps managers allocate resources and focus monitoring on activities where delay threatens completion.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis
fragments.text:
Total float = latest finish - earliest start - duration
Free float = earliest start of next activity - earliest start of current activity - duration

fragments.label: CPA evaluation
fragments.text: Benefits: shows dependencies, critical tasks, minimum duration and scheduling flexibility. Limitations: activity times are estimates; resource constraints are not automatically solved; complex projects change and require updates; unexpected events can create a new critical path.

Financial statements communicate performance over a period and financial position at a date. At A2 you must interpret the statement of profit or loss and statement of financial position, understand relationships between them, and know inventory valuation using net realisable value and straight-line depreciation.

fragments.label: Net realisable value
fragments.text: Expected selling value of inventory less the costs necessary to complete/sell it.

fragments.label: Depreciation
fragments.text: Allocation of a non-current asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.

fragments.label: Retained earnings
fragments.text: Profits retained in the business rather than distributed to owners.

fragments.label: Statement of profit or loss
fragments.text: Shows performance over a period. Typical flow: revenue -> cost of sales -> gross profit -> operating expenses -> profit from operations -> finance/tax/other items -> profit for the year. Trace a change through every affected subtotal rather than discussing one line only.

fragments.label: Statement of financial position
fragments.text: A snapshot at a specific date showing non-current assets, current assets, current liabilities, net current assets, non-current liabilities and equity/reserves. It indicates resources controlled and financing obligations.

fragments.label: How the statements connect
fragments.text: Retained profit can increase equity/reserves. Depreciation reduces profit and reduces the carrying value of non-current assets. Inventory valuation affects both current assets and cost of sales/profit. The statements therefore must be analysed together.

fragments.label: Inventory valuation and NRV
fragments.text: Inventory may become damaged, obsolete or fall in selling price. Reporting it above what can be recovered overstates assets and potentially profit. NRV reflects expected recoverable amount after costs needed to complete/sell.

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: The same depreciation expense is charged each year across useful life. It reduces reported profit and the carrying amount of the asset but is not itself a current-year cash payment.

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: Annual depreciation = (cost - residual value) / useful life

fragments.label: Using statements strategically
fragments.text: Statements provide evidence of profitability, liquidity, asset use and financing but are mainly historical. Managers/investors should combine them with ratios, cash-flow forecasts and non-financial information.

Ratio analysis converts financial-statement data into indicators of liquidity, profitability, efficiency, gearing and investor return. Calculation is only the first step: top answers compare, diagnose causes, explain consequences, propose actions and recognise limitations.

fragments.label: Liquidity
fragments.text: Ability to meet short-term obligations when they fall due.

fragments.label: Profitability
fragments.text: Ability to generate profit relative to revenue or capital employed.

fragments.label: Efficiency
fragments.text: How effectively working capital/assets are managed to support operations.

fragments.label: Gearing
fragments.text: Extent to which long-term capital relies on non-current debt.

fragments.label: ROCE
fragments.text: Operating profit generated as a percentage of capital employed.

fragments.label: P/E ratio
fragments.text: Market price per share relative to earnings per share, often reflecting market expectations.

fragments.label: Liquidity ratios
fragments.text: Current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities. Acid test removes inventory because it may be less liquid. Very low ratios can signal payment risk; very high ratios may signal inefficient working capital. Industry context matters.

fragments.label: Liquidity ratios
fragments.text:
Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities
Acid test = (Current assets - Inventory) / Current liabilities

fragments.label: Profitability ratios
fragments.text: Gross margin reflects selling price and direct cost of sales; operating margin also reflects operating expenses. ROCE relates operating profit to long-term capital committed.

fragments.label: Profitability ratios
fragments.text:
Gross profit margin = Gross profit / Revenue x100
Operating profit margin = Profit from operations / Revenue x100
ROCE = Profit from operations / Capital employed x100

fragments.label: Efficiency ratios
fragments.text: Inventory turnover indicates how often inventory is sold/used. Receivables days estimates collection speed from credit customers; payables days estimates payment time to suppliers. Faster is not automatically better if it causes stockouts, customer loss or supplier conflict.

fragments.label: Efficiency ratios
fragments.text:
Inventory turnover = Cost of sales / Average inventory
Receivables days = Trade receivables / Credit sales x365
Payables days = Trade payables / Credit purchases x365

fragments.label: Gearing
fragments.text: Higher gearing means greater reliance on long-term debt and therefore more fixed interest/repayment risk. Debt can still improve owners' returns when operating returns exceed borrowing cost. Context includes cash-flow stability and interest rates.

fragments.label: Gearing
fragments.text: Gearing (%) = Non-current liabilities / Capital employed x100

fragments.label: Investor ratios
fragments.text: P/E indicates how highly the market values earnings; dividend yield compares cash dividend with market price; dividend cover indicates how many times profit covers the dividend and therefore how much safety/retention exists.

fragments.label: Investor ratios
fragments.text:
P/E = Market price per share / Earnings per share
Dividend yield = Dividend per share / Market price per share x100
Dividend cover = Profit for the year / Annual dividend

fragments.label: Interpreting and improving
fragments.text: Use previous years, targets, competitors or industry averages. Then move from result -> possible cause -> consequence -> action. Improvements may have trade-offs: tighter receivables collection improves cash but may reduce customer attractiveness.

fragments.label: Limitations
fragments.text: Ratios rely on historical accounts and accounting policies, can be distorted by one-off items/inflation/window dressing, omit many intangibles and can be misleading across different business models. They identify symptoms, not proven causes.

Investment appraisal compares long-term projects using payback, Accounting Rate of Return (ARR) and Net Present Value (NPV). You must calculate each method, understand what it measures, compare its strengths/limitations and integrate qualitative strategic factors before recommending a project.

fragments.label: Payback period
fragments.text: Time required for cumulative net cash inflows to recover the initial investment.

fragments.label: ARR
fragments.text: Average annual accounting profit as a percentage of average investment.

fragments.label: Discount factor
fragments.text: Factor converting a future cash flow into present value.

fragments.label: NPV
fragments.text: Total present value of future net cash flows minus the initial investment.

fragments.label: Time value of money
fragments.text: The principle that money available now is worth more than the same nominal amount received later.

fragments.label: Why appraise investments
fragments.text: Major capital projects tie up finance for years and involve uncertain future returns. Appraisal provides structured evidence on liquidity, return and value, helping compare alternatives and justify resource allocation.

fragments.label: Payback
fragments.text: Add net cash inflows until initial cost is recovered. Short payback is useful when liquidity/risk/technology change matter, but ignores cash flows after payback and usually ignores time value of money.

fragments.label: Payback
fragments.text: If £100k is invested and £80k has been recovered after year 2, with £40k in year 3, another £20k/£40k=0.5 year -> payback 2.5 years.

fragments.label: ARR
fragments.text: Uses average annual accounting profit and average investment, producing a familiar percentage. It considers profitability over the project life but uses accounting profit rather than cash and ignores timing of returns.

fragments.label: ARR
fragments.text: ARR = Average annual profit / Average investment x100

fragments.label: NPV
fragments.text: Discount each future net cash flow at the required rate and subtract the initial cost. Positive NPV means discounted inflows exceed the initial investment at that required return. Higher NPV generally adds more financial value, but forecasts and discount rate may be wrong.

fragments.label: NPV
fragments.text: NPV = sum of discounted net cash inflows - initial investment

fragments.label: Qualitative factors
fragments.text: Strategic fit, brand, employee impact, environmental effect, technological flexibility, legal constraints, risk and competitor reaction can outweigh a small numerical advantage. Quantitative appraisal supports judgement rather than replacing it.

fragments.label: Comparing methods
fragments.text: Payback emphasises speed/liquidity, ARR accounting profitability and NPV timing/opportunity cost. Rankings can differ. Strong evaluation asks which criterion matters most for the business's objectives/risk and how reliable the forecasts are.

Finance and accounting strategy uses published financial information to support long-term decisions. You must assess performance over time/against competitors and analyse how debt/equity, dividend decisions, business growth and other strategies affect ratios. The key evaluation point is that accounts are useful evidence but not perfect objective truth.

fragments.label: Annual report
fragments.text: Financial statements plus narrative/governance/risk information reporting company performance and position.

fragments.label: Debt finance
fragments.text: Borrowed long-term finance with contractual interest/repayment.

fragments.label: Equity finance
fragments.text: Finance provided by owners/shareholders, affecting ownership and shareholder returns rather than creating contractual interest.

fragments.label: Dividend policy
fragments.text: The approach to distributing profit to shareholders versus retaining it for reinvestment.

fragments.label: Window dressing
fragments.text: Actions/accounting presentation intended to make reported position/performance look more favourable around reporting time.

fragments.label: Using accounts strategically
fragments.text: Accounts reveal profitability, liquidity, efficiency, financing and resource position. Weak liquidity may constrain expansion; strong ROCE may support investment; falling margins may trigger cost/price/product changes. Financial evidence should be combined with market, HR and operations information.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholders
fragments.text: Annual reports can contain statements, strategic commentary, risk, governance, sustainability and audit information. Investors, lenders, employees, suppliers and managers use different information. Narrative sections provide context but management may emphasise favourable aspects.

fragments.label: Debt versus equity
fragments.text: Debt avoids ownership dilution and can be cost-effective, but raises gearing and fixed interest/repayment risk. Equity can reduce debt pressure and strengthen finance capacity but dilutes control/earnings per share and may create dividend expectations. Choice depends on cash-flow stability, interest rates, investor appetite and desired control.

fragments.label: Dividend strategy
fragments.text: Higher dividends may attract income-seeking shareholders and signal confidence but reduce retained funds for investment/liquidity. Lower dividends support self-financed growth but may disappoint investors. Dividend decisions affect yield, cover and retained earnings.

fragments.label: Growth and ratio effects
fragments.text: Expansion can initially weaken liquidity or raise gearing because working capital/capital expenditure must be financed. Later economies/productivity/revenue may improve margins and ROCE. A short-term ratio decline after strategic investment is not automatically failure.

fragments.label: Limitations of published accounts
fragments.text: Accounts are mostly historical, use estimates/accounting policies, can be affected by inflation, one-offs and window dressing, and omit many intangible strengths. Cross-company comparisons can be distorted by different business models/policies. Ratios diagnose symptoms but do not prove causes.

fragments.label: Integrated judgement
fragments.text: A finance strategy should support overall objectives. A business pursuing fast growth may accept temporarily higher gearing; a mature firm with stable cash might return more cash to shareholders. The recommendation must fit risk, cash generation and strategic opportunity.
A focused revision guide to atomic structure.

fragments.label: Subatomic particles
fragments.text: Protons (+1), neutrons (0), electrons (−1, negligible mass). Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons. Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron count.

fragments.label: Ionisation energy trends
fragments.text: Increases across a period (more protons, same shell); decreases down a group (extra shielding shells, greater distance).
Use moles to balance equations and calculate reacting masses, gas volumes and solution concentrations.
A focused revision guide to chemical bonding.

fragments.label: Bond types
fragments.text: Ionic — electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Covalent — shared electron pair(s). Metallic — delocalised electrons attracted to a lattice of positive ions.

fragments.label: Intermolecular forces
fragments.text: Weakest to strongest: van der Waals < permanent dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding (needs H bonded directly to N, O or F).
Use the particle model and the ideal gas equation, and understand the structures of solids.
A focused revision guide to chemical energetics.

fragments.label: Enthalpy change ΔH
fragments.text: Exothermic releases energy (ΔH negative); endothermic absorbs energy (ΔH positive).

fragments.label: Hess's law
fragments.text: Enthalpy change is independent of route. Draw a cycle via a common intermediate and add/subtract arrows to find the unknown ΔH.
Assign oxidation states, balance redox equations, and understand the process of electrolysis.
A focused revision guide to equilibria.

fragments.label: Dynamic equilibrium & Le Chatelier
fragments.text: Forward/reverse rates become equal at equilibrium. A disturbance shifts equilibrium to partially oppose the change — more reactant → shifts to products; more pressure → shifts to fewer gas moles; more heat → shifts endothermic direction.

fragments.label: Kc
fragments.text: A catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium but does not change its position or Kc.

Reaction kinetics explains why some reactions happen faster than others, using collision theory as the underlying model. At AS level the focus is qualitative — explaining rate changes in terms of collision frequency and the proportion of particles with enough energy to react — while the quantitative treatment (rate equations, orders of reaction) comes in the A2 topic.

fragments.label: Activation energy (Ea)
fragments.text: The minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur.

fragments.label: Collision theory
fragments.text: The model stating that a reaction only occurs when particles collide with energy ≥ Ea and in the correct orientation.

fragments.label: Catalyst
fragments.text: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, without itself being used up.

fragments.label: Collision theory & activation energy
fragments.text: Not every collision between particles leads to a reaction — only those with enough energy (≥ Ea) and the correct orientation actually react. This is why increasing the frequency or energy of collisions increases the rate.

fragments.label: Collision theory & activation energy
fragments.text: Weak collision (low energy) → particles bounce apart, no reaction

fragments.label: Collision theory & activation energy
fragments.text: Collision with E ≥ Ea and correct orientation → bonds break/form, reaction occurs

fragments.label: Factors affecting rate
fragments.text: Concentration/pressure increase the number of particles per unit volume, so collisions happen more often. Surface area (for solids) exposes more particles to collide with. Temperature increases both the speed of particles and, more importantly, the proportion with energy ≥ Ea. A catalyst offers a lower-energy pathway, so a larger fraction of collisions now exceed the (lower) activation energy.

fragments.label: Factors affecting rate
fragments.text: Doubling the concentration of a reactant roughly doubles collision frequency (for a first-order reactant)

fragments.label: Factors affecting rate
fragments.text: A platinum catalyst in the Contact process lowers Ea for SO₂ oxidation

fragments.label: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
fragments.text: This is a graph of the number of particles (y-axis) against their kinetic energy (x-axis) at a given temperature — an asymmetric curve starting at the origin, rising to a peak, then tailing off. Raising the temperature shifts the peak right and flattens/broadens the curve, while the total area under the curve stays the same (same number of particles). Crucially, the area under the curve beyond Ea — the fraction of particles that can react — increases sharply even for a modest temperature rise.

fragments.label: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
fragments.text: At T1, only a small area of the curve lies beyond Ea

fragments.label: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
fragments.text: At T2 > T1, the curve flattens/shifts right, and a much larger area lies beyond Ea, even though Ea itself hasn't changed
Rate increases only if collisions occur more often AND/OR more collisions exceed Ea
Catalyst = lower Ea via alternative pathway, not used up
Temperature ↑ → M-B curve flattens/shifts right → more particles exceed Ea

title: An introduction to AS Level organic chemistry

fragments.text: A focused revision guide to an introduction to as level organic chemistry.

fragments.label: Naming & functional groups
fragments.text: Homologous series share a general formula and functional group. Suffixes: -ane (alkane), -ene (alkene), -ol (alcohol), -oic acid (carboxylic acid), -one (ketone).

fragments.label: Isomerism
fragments.text: Structural isomers — same molecular formula, different arrangement. Stereoisomers — same structural formula, different spatial arrangement (E/Z around a C=C).

fragments.label: Mechanisms
fragments.text: Curly arrows must start from a bond or lone pair and point to where the new bond/charge forms.
